extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of combustion turbine EGUs, regulated industry, state agencies, environmental stakeholders, and commenters on the EPA NSPS rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and BSER (best system of emission reduction) determinations for newly constructed and reconstructed stationary combustion turbines (EGUs) under the NSPS, organized by subcategory (low load, intermediate load, base load). Provides the EPA's rationale, evidence, and specific performance standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for Low Load Subcategory — use of lower-emitting fuels
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is finalizing that the use of fuels with an emissions rate of less than 160 lb CO2/MMBtu (i.e., lower-emitting fuels) meets the BSER requirements for the low load (peaking) subcategory. The EPA identifies natural gas, Nos. 1 and 2 fuel oils, and other fuels currently specified in 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT (and finalizes inclusion of hydrogen) as qualifying lower-emitting fuels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: lower-emitting fuels are technically feasible, widely used (natural gas comprised the majority of heat input for simple cycle turbines), have minimal incremental cost, and do not have significant adverse energy or non-air quality impacts. EPA explains that low-load units have variable operation (multiple starts/stops, part-load operation) making a uniform output-based standard impracticable. Therefore efficient design/operation is not appropriate as BSER for low load. The rule narrows the low load definition and adds low-GHG hydrogen to the uniform fuels criteria (40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTTa) to simplify recordkeeping/reporting for turbines electing to burn hydrogen. EPA did not finalize CCS or hydrogen co-firing as BSER for low load due to technical/cost/infrastructure concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-input (fuel-based) compliance approach for low load
rubrics_metrics.description: For the non-base/low load subcategory EPA previously (2015 NSPS) established a heat input-based standard (e.g., 120 lb CO2/MMBtu) because output-based standards could not reasonably be applied to these units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as practical approach because emissions rates of low-capacity-factor units depend heavily on operation (starts/stops, part-load) not design efficiency. This supports selecting fuel-use/heat-input metrics rather than output-based standards for low load.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for Intermediate Load Subcategory — highly efficient simple cycle technology plus best operating and maintenance practices
rubrics_metrics.description: For intermediate load combustion turbines, the EPA finalizes as BSER the use of high-efficiency simple cycle turbine technology in combination with the best operating and maintenance (O&M) practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What counts as 'highly efficient' and best O&M: manufacturers increase firing temperature, pressure ratios, use intercooling, etc.; design efficiencies for simple cycle turbines range from ~33–40%. Best O&M examples include proper maintenance of flow path components and inlet air cooling to reduce performance losses. EPA finds the technology adequately demonstrated, commercially available, and capable of implementation at reasonable cost (EPA estimates ~10% higher capital cost and ~8% less fuel for high-efficiency simple cycle turbines; LCOE comparisons at relevant capacity factors provided). EPA determined corresponding output-based standard of performance for intermediate load of 1,170 lb CO2/MWh-gross.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-emitting fuels are not BSER for intermediate load
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not propose and is not finalizing lower-emitting fuels as the BSER for intermediate load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: at higher capacity factors, highly efficient generation achieves materially greater GHG reductions than fuel-switching alone. EPA concluded lower-emitting fuels would achieve few reductions compared to highly efficient generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated (evidence criterion for BSER)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's test for 'adequately demonstrated' includes whether the technology has been demonstrated by multiple facilities for decades, improvements are incremental, operation/maintenance practices are not fundamentally altered, and the performance levels have been achieved by recently constructed units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify that both highly efficient simple cycle and combined cycle designs are commercially available and that standards based on them are achievable. Technologies lacking sufficient field demonstration (e.g., some proposed novel technologies) are not included as BSER until further evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs — reasonableness and cost-effectiveness assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates whether incremental capital and operating costs of the candidate BSER are reasonable and cost-effective, including LCOE impacts, fuel savings, and uncertainty in cost estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: high-efficiency simple cycle turbines estimated ~10% higher capital cost and 8% lower fuel use; at certain capacity factors this yields lower LCOE. EPA provides per-MWh and $/ton compliance cost examples at 20% and 15% capacity factors and notes substantial uncertainty in estimates. For base load combined cycle, EPA cites 1.9% higher capital cost and 2.6% lower fuel use, with fuel savings offsetting capital over a 30-year life at ≥40% capacity factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational flexibility and startup/shutdown characteristics (applicability criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers operational flexibility—startup times, minimum run times, starts/year limits, and ability to provide grid services—when determining whether a technology can serve as BSER for a subcategory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: simple cycle hot-start to full load in 5–8 minutes vs combined cycle 30–90 minutes (fast/conventional); cold starts: simple cycle 10 min vs combined cycle 120–250 min; minimum run times and downtime differ (e.g., simple cycle aeroderivative min run 1 min, combined cycle 120 min). EPA used these characteristics to conclude combined cycle is generally not appropriate as the BSER for intermediate load units because it may not provide the required flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of steam injection (evaluated technology but not BSER)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated steam injection (use of a relatively simple and low-cost HRSG to produce steam injected into compressor or combustion chamber) as a potential technology for intermediate load turbines but did not determine it to be the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: improved efficiency, increased output, reduced NOx, fast start, good part-load performance. Cons/limits: added complexity and capital cost relative to simple cycle, pressure drop across HRSG can reduce efficiency when steam injection not operating. EPA concluded steam injection is promising but not adequately demonstrated or analyzed sufficiently in the proposal to include as BSER at this time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-GHG hydrogen co-firing and CCS — evaluated but not BSER for low/intermediate load
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not propose and is not finalizing CCS or low-GHG hydrogen co-firing as the BSER for low or intermediate load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale for CCS exclusion: post-combustion amine-based capture requires cooled exhaust (typically via HRSG), which is integral to combined cycle plants and not simple cycle units; high costs for low load. Rationale for hydrogen exclusion: not all new turbines can co-fire high hydrogen fractions, infrastructure issues, and low utilization of low-load units may make co-firing not cost-effective. EPA leaves open future evaluation for other technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for Base Load Subcategory — first component: high-efficiency combined cycle technology plus best O&M practices
rubrics_metrics.description: For base load combustion turbines, the first component of the BSER is use of high-efficiency combined cycle technology in combination with best operating and maintenance practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finds highly efficient combined cycle designs adequately demonstrated. EPA proposes less stringent standards for smaller base load turbines (base load ratings < 2,000 MMBtu/h) due to HRSG efficiency differences. EPA assessed costs (slightly higher capital cost, fuel savings that fully offset capital at capacity factors ≥40% over 30 years) and non-air impacts. EPA determined a standard reflecting this BSER of 800 lb CO2/MWh-gross for base load turbines.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for Base Load Subcategory — second component: 90 percent CCS beginning in 2032
rubrics_metrics.description: For base load stationary combustion turbines the second component of the BSER is 90 percent carbon capture and storage (CCS) beginning in 2032 (i.e., a two-component BSER: highly efficient generation + 90% CCS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors the Agency's approach for fossil steam EGUs where post-combustion partial CCS was part of the BSER. The rule text (Table 3) lists 'Highly Efficient Combined Cycle Generation Plus 90 Percent CCS Beginning in 2032' as the second component for base load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates whether the BSER will have significant adverse non-air quality health/environmental impacts or adverse energy requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's finding: use of highly efficient generation reduces non-air pollutants and energy requirements (more electricity per unit fuel reduces emissions of all pollutants). EPA concluded designation of highly efficient generation as BSER will not have significant adverse impacts on nationwide electricity supply, prices, or sector structure; additional costs are small and partly offset by reduced fuel costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of reductions in CO2 emissions and methodology for estimating reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assesses the magnitude of expected CO2 reductions from the standard-of-performance reflecting the BSER and documents the estimation method and projected annual reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: EPA determined standards reflecting BSERs of 1,170 lb CO2/MWh-gross (intermediate load) and 800 lb CO2/MWh-gross (base load). EPA estimated annual reductions for intermediate load (31,000 tons CO2 and 8 tons NOX using retrospective application to 2015–2022 builds) and for base load (313,000 tons CO2 and 23 tons NOX initially, increasing in subsequent years). Method: EPA compared observed emissions rates of recently constructed units to the BSER-based standard, calculated required percent reductions, applied to capacity factors, summed and averaged over years evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of development and implementation of technology (innovation-support factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers whether selecting a BSER will promote further development and adoption of improved control or generation technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA reasoned that setting standards based on the performance of the most efficient units will promote penetration of the most efficient designs (e.g., high-efficiency simple cycle turbines) throughout the industry, thus supporting selection of highly efficient generation as BSER even apart from cost/emissions considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with other BSERs and avoidance of rebound-effect risks
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA contrasts 'highly efficient generation' with prior BSER determinations (e.g., heat rate improvements (HRI) in the ACE Rule) and considers potential behavioral/economic effects like the 'rebound effect' when assessing BSER appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains HRI for existing coal EGUs could cause increased overall CO2 via rebound (more dispatch hours), whereas new highly efficient combustion turbines are more likely to displace higher-emitting sources (coal or less-efficient turbines) rather than renewables, reducing the risk of adverse rebound outcomes. This comparative reasoning supports choosing highly efficient generation as BSER for new/reconstructed combustion turbines.
